artiest/jean-paul-de-coster.text:
Jean-Paul De Coster is a Belgian producer and songwriter from Antwerp. Together with his fellow Antwerp native Phil Wilde, he made dance music in the early 1990s in their own studio. Their first collaboration appeared under the name Bizz Nizz, with the single Don't Miss the Party Line, which reached the top 10 in England. It whetted their appetite for more.

In May 1991 De Coster and Wilde made an instrumental track, Get Ready for This, which became a club hit. They asked the Dutch rapper Ray Slijngaard to put a rap on it. He came back with a tape on which Anita Doth, an acquaintance from the Amsterdam nightlife scene, also sang. That is how 2 Unlimited came about. De Coster and Wilde wrote and produced the music on the Belgian label Byte Records. After Get Ready for This came Twilight Zone (1992), No Limit and Tribal Dance (1993) and The Real Thing (1994). The albums Get Ready!, No Limits! and Real Things were great successes all over Europe. When Ray and Anita left in 1996, De Coster and Wilde looked for new female singers, because they held the rights to the name.

De Coster's music was Eurodance: fast beats, hard synthesizer riffs, short raps and a singalong chorus that keeps coming back. British critics found it too simple, but the crowds in clubs and at sporting events did not. De Coster shows how in dance music the producers are often the real creators, while the public mostly knows the faces on stage. In 2012 he began working with Ray and Anita again.
artiest/jean-paul-de-coster.listen: Listen to No Limit (1993) by 2 Unlimited. Notice how the track is almost entirely built on repetition: the same synthesizer riff, the same beat and a chorus of just a few words.

artiest/jean-philippe-rameau.text: Jean-Philippe Rameau was a provincial organist before he made his name in 1722 with his Traité de l'harmonie. In it he described chords as stacks of thirds above a root, an idea on which the theory of harmony still rests. Only around the age of fifty did he write his first opera, Hippolyte et Aricie, and with it he gave the French opera of Lully a richer sound. His Les Sauvages arose after a performance by two dancing Native Americans in Paris.
artiest/jean-philippe-rameau.listen: Listen to Les Sauvages and hear how the stamping, constantly recurring dance melody swells until the chorus joins in.

artiest/jean-sibelius.text:
Jean Sibelius was a Finnish composer of the late Romantic and early modern period. He was born in 1865 in Hämeenlinna, then part of the Grand Duchy of Finland within the Russian Empire. He first wanted to become a violinist, then studied composition in Helsinki, Berlin and Vienna, and in 1892 married Aino Järnefelt. In 1904 the family moved to the house Ainola near Järvenpää, where he lived for the rest of his life.

At its core is a cycle of seven symphonies. He also wrote the Violin Concerto, the choral work Kullervo, Finlandia, the Karelia Suite, Valse triste and The Swan of Tuonela, part of the Lemminkäinen Suite. Much of his music springs from nature, Nordic mythology and the Kalevala, the Finnish national epic. His sound is sombre and broad, with long lines and a large orchestra that often sounds like a landscape.

In the years of Russian rule his music contributed to a stronger Finnish national awareness, and he is still regarded as the greatest composer of his country. After 1926, with the symphonic poem Tapiola and the music for The Tempest, he wrote almost nothing more. That silence of Järvenpää lasted thirty years. He died in 1957. His work is performed and recorded widely around the world.
artiest/jean-sibelius.listen: Listen to Finlandia and notice how it begins with heavy, menacing brass chords and later moves into a broad, singing melody.

artiest/jean-yves-thibaudet.text:
Jean-Yves Thibaudet is a French pianist, born in 1961 in Lyon. His mother, herself a fairly accomplished pianist, introduced him to the piano. At five he went to the Lyon conservatoire, at seven he gave his first performance and at twelve he won a gold medal there. He then studied in Paris with Aldo Ciccolini and Lucette Descaves, and at eighteen he won the Young Concert Artists Auditions in New York.

He has played with the great orchestras of Berlin, Amsterdam, London, New York, Chicago and other cities and was the first permanent artist in residence at the Boston Symphony Orchestra, the Seattle Symphony Orchestra and the Colburn School in Los Angeles. He made more than fifty recordings, most of them for Decca. These include a box set of the complete piano works of Erik Satie, released on the composer's 150th anniversary. He is known for his interpretation of French music, but also plays Liszt, Rachmaninoff, Gershwin and opera transcriptions.

He also ventured into jazz. The albums Conversations with Bill Evans from 1997 and Reflections on Duke from 1999 contain arrangements and elaborations of improvisations by Bill Evans and Duke Ellington. His playing can also be heard on film music, including Atonement, which won an Oscar for best score. In this way he stands on the border between classical concert life, jazz and film.
artiest/jean-yves-thibaudet.listen: Listen to a piece from Conversations with Bill Evans or Reflections on Duke and notice how a classically trained pianist makes room for jazz harmony and free phrasing.

artiest/jeanne-lee.text:
Jeanne Lee was an American jazz singer, poet and composer. She was born in 1939 in New York. Her father was a concert and church singer. At Bard College she studied child psychology, literature and dance, and there she made choreographies for classical and jazz compositions. Her first album, The Newest Sound Around, appeared in 1962.

In the 1960s she explored sound poetry, happenings and art in the spirit of Fluxus. She made music for sound poems by poets such as Dick Higgins and Alison Knowles and was active in the Californian art world. At the end of that decade she returned to jazz. In 1976 she represented African American spirituals in John Cage's Apartment House 1776, written for the American bicentennial. That experience prompted her to write longer works of her own, such as the jazz oratorio Prayer for Our Time.

Lee mastered a wide range of vocal styles and worked with many innovators, including Gunter Hampel, Andrew Cyrille, Ran Blake, Carla Bley, Anthony Braxton, Marion Brown, Archie Shepp and Mal Waldron. She sang on a large number of Hampel's albums and recorded for labels such as BYG Actuel, ECM and Black Saint. She also taught and wrote a textbook on the history of jazz for primary schools. She died of cancer in 2000. Her importance lies in the way she used the voice as a free instrument, at the intersection of jazz, poetry and dance.
artiest/jeanne-lee.listen: Listen to a recording by Jeanne Lee with Archie Shepp or Mal Waldron and notice how her voice sometimes sings, sometimes almost speaks, and thereby plays along like an instrument.

artiest/jeannie-robertson.text:
Jeannie Robertson, in full Regina Christina Robertson, was a Scottish folk singer. She was born in 1908 in Aberdeen, the daughter of a bagpiper, Donald, and a singer, Maria Stewart, and died in 1975. In Aberdeen a plaque commemorates her home on Hilton Road. She learned her songs in the traditional way, orally, without the influence of radio or books.

In 1953 the folklorist Hamish Henderson sought her out in Aberdeen. According to tradition she only let him in after he had named the first line of Child ballad no. 163, The Battle of Harlaw. In November of that year Alan Lomax recorded her in his London apartment, together with other singers such as Jean Ritchie and Margaret Barry. There she sang, among other songs, My Son David and Andrew Lammie, a ballad of more than thirteen minutes. Many of those recordings appeared in 1975 as The Queen Among the Heather. In 1958 Henderson recorded her again, in Edinburgh, for Up the Dee and Doon The Don. She also performed at the Blairgowrie Festival, from 1965, and besides classic ballads she sang bawdy songs.

She became known for her version of I'm a Man You Don't Meet Every Day, also called Jock Stewart, which was later covered by The Dubliners and The Pogues. Her daughter Lizzie Higgins and her nephew Stanley Robertson carried on the tradition. She is regarded as one of the most important bearers of the Scottish ballad tradition and as a source for the folk revival of the 1950s and 1960s.
artiest/jeannie-robertson.listen: Listen to My Son David and notice the voice: she sings unaccompanied, with a sharp, free rhythm. Hear how she stretches the phrases and tells the story.

artiest/jeff-barry.text:
Jeff Barry is an American songwriter, singer and producer, born in 1938 as Joel Adelberg in Brooklyn, New York. He grew up partly in New Jersey. His first big success as a writer came in 1960 with Tell Laura I Love Her, a hit for Ray Peterson and in England for Ricky Valance. In 1962 he married Ellie Greenwich, and from then on they wrote together.

The couple became one of the most important writing teams of the 1960s. For the producer Phil Spector they wrote Da Doo Ron Ron and Then He Kissed Me for The Crystals, Be My Baby for The Ronettes and later River Deep Mountain High for Ike & Tina Turner. Spector turned their songs into his Wall of Sound. At Red Bird Records, the label of Leiber and Stoller, they wrote and produced Chapel of Love for The Dixie Cups and Leader of the Pack for The Shangri-Las. Do Wah Diddy Diddy, a big hit for Manfred Mann, was also theirs. In 1965 they divorced, but they went on working together for a while. Barry then produced Neil Diamond's I'm a Believer for The Monkees and, with Andy Kim, wrote Sugar, Sugar for The Archies.

Barry belongs to the professional songwriters who shaped the pop of the 1960s, often in duos who made a trade of writing. His songs are short and catchy, with choruses that stick at once. Later he also wrote country hits and tunes for television series.
artiest/jeff-barry.listen: Listen to Be My Baby (1963) by The Ronettes. Notice the simple, recognisable drum rhythm at the start and how layer after layer of sound is then added, until a full wall of sound.

artiest/jeff-beck.text:
Jeff Beck was an English guitarist, born in 1944 in Wallington, Surrey. As a child he sang in a church choir and built his first guitars himself from a cigar box and a fence post. After school he studied at the art college in Wimbledon. He played in various bands and in 1965 joined the Yardbirds, as the successor to Eric Clapton. Jimmy Page had recommended him.

He stayed with the Yardbirds for twenty months. In that time they recorded most of their hits, and the group made the album Roger the Engineer. He was dismissed because during an American tour he often failed to turn up, and because of his perfectionism and tantrums. He then founded the Jeff Beck Group and later Beck, Bogert and Appice.

In 1975 he chose instrumental music with an emphasis on an innovative guitar sound. The albums Blow by Blow from 1975 and Wired from 1976 were successful. His work extended into blues rock, hard rock, jazz fusion and a mixture of guitar and electronics. Beck won eight Grammys in total and was inducted twice into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame: as a member of the Yardbirds and as a solo artist. He often ranked high on lists of the best guitarists and was called a guitarist's guitarist. He died in 2023.
artiest/jeff-beck.listen: Listen to an instrumental track from Blow by Blow and notice how the guitar tells the whole story without a singer, with bending notes and a singing tone of its own.

artiest/jeff-lorber.text:
Jeff Lorber is an American keyboard player, composer and producer, born in 1952 in Cheltenham, Pennsylvania, the same suburb as Michael and Randy Brecker. He began on piano at four, played in R&B bands as a teenager and studied at the Berklee College of Music, where he met the guitarist John Scofield.

His first group was the Jeff Lorber Fusion, which released the debut album The Jeff Lorber Fusion on Inner City Records in 1977. He recorded five studio albums under that name. They sounded funky and owed much to the jazz fusion of Herbie Hancock, Weather Report and Return to Forever. In 1984 the solo album In the Heat of the Night followed. Later that year, with the duo David Frank and Mic Murphy, known as The System, he produced the album Step by Step. The title song, written with Anita Pointer of the Pointer Sisters, reached number 31 on the American R&B chart.

Lorber became an established name in smooth jazz. His music was often used in the forecasts of The Weather Channel and his keyboard work can even be heard in the computer game Castlevania: Symphony of the Night. He worked as a producer and session musician for, among others, Dave Koz, Herb Alpert and Laura Branigan. In 2018 he won his first Grammy, for the album Prototype by the Jeff Lorber Fusion. He is an example of how fusion developed from complex jazz rock into a more accessible, smoother sound.
artiest/jeff-lorber.listen: Listen to Step by Step and notice the electronic keyboards and the tight funk rhythms of the 1980s.

artiest/jeff-lynne.text:
Jeff Lynne is an English singer, songwriter and producer, born in 1947 in Birmingham. He was strongly influenced by the Beatles. He began in 1963 with the Andicaps, joined the Chads and from 1966 to 1970 was founder and regular songwriter of the Idle Race. In 1968 he was allowed to watch for an hour at Abbey Road as the Beatles recorded the White Album, an experience he never forgot.

In 1970, at the invitation of Roy Wood, he joined the Move. Together with Wood and drummer Bev Bevan he built a band there that was meant to unite rock and classical music: Electric Light Orchestra, ELO for short. The group wanted to carry on where the Beatles had left off. From 1972, after Wood's departure, Lynne wrote all the music. The hits include Evil Woman, Livin' Thing, Telephone Line, Mr. Blue Sky and Don't Bring Me Down.

After 1986 he became chiefly a producer. In 1988 he formed the supergroup Traveling Wilburys with George Harrison, Bob Dylan, Roy Orbison and Tom Petty. For the Beatles he co-produced the singles Free as a Bird, Real Love and Now and Then, made from demos by John Lennon. In 2017 he was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame with ELO. His importance lies in the idea of a rock band with strings, built on the meticulous studio technique of a producer who began as a band member.
artiest/jeff-lynne.listen: Listen to Mr. Blue Sky by ELO and notice how pop melody, choral singing and strings are layered over one another, like a small studio opera.

artiest/jeff-mills.text:
Jeff Mills is an American DJ, producer and composer, born in 1963 in Detroit. He began in the early 1980s as a radio DJ under the name The Wizard. He used tricks such as beat juggling and scratching and in his late-night radio shows played local techno, by among others Derrick May, Kevin Saunderson and Juan Atkins.

In the 1980s he co-founded the techno collective Underground Resistance with Mad Mike Banks and Robert Hood. The group performed only in ski masks and black combat clothing and linked the sound of early Detroit techno to the social and political conditions of the city after the economic decline of the 1980s. In 1991 Mills went his own way. He lived successively in New York, Berlin, where he DJed at the club Tresor, and Chicago. There in 1992 he started the label Axis with Robert Hood, with sublabels such as Purpose Maker and Tomorrow. His techno sounded more minimal than much of what was being made at the time.

After that he kept searching for new forms. The album Blue Potential from 2006 captures a live concert with the seventy-piece Montpellier Philharmonic Orchestra. In 2013 he made Where Light Ends, inspired by the journey into space of the Japanese astronaut Mamoru Mohri. He made films and in 2018 recorded an EP with the drummer Tony Allen. Mills is regarded as one of the most important names of Detroit techno.
artiest/jeff-mills.listen: Listen to a track from Waveform Transmission, Volume 1 and notice how few elements there are: a hard, repeating drum machine and small changes that build the tension.

artiest/jeff-porcaro.text:
Jeff Porcaro was an American drummer and songwriter, born in 1954 in Hartford, Connecticut. He was the eldest son of the Los Angeles session percussionist Joe Porcaro, and grew up in the San Fernando Valley. He began drumming at seven, first with lessons from his father. At seventeen he was already playing in Sonny & Cher's touring band. He then became a much sought-after studio musician, including on three Steely Dan albums, among them Katy Lied (1975).

Together with his brother Steve and childhood friends David Paich and Steve Lukather he founded Toto. The band had hits such as Hold the Line, Rosanna and Africa, which Porcaro wrote with Paich. The album Toto IV (1982) became their greatest success. For Rosanna Porcaro devised a famous rhythm: a half-time shuffle in which he blended the shuffle of Bernard Purdie with the groove of John Bonham in Fool in the Rain. Alongside Toto he kept doing session work, and played on tracks from Michael Jackson's Thriller and on records by Boz Scaggs and Dire Straits.

Porcaro was regarded as one of the most valued studio drummers of his time. His playing was tight and relaxed at once, with small details that let a track breathe. The sound of pop drums in the 1980s was largely his sound. He died in 1992 at the age of 38 of a heart attack.
artiest/jeff-porcaro.listen: Listen to Africa (1982) by Toto. Notice how Porcaro plays a light, straight groove beneath all kinds of layers of percussion, so that the track stays light and open.

artiest/jeff-tain-watts.text:
Jeff Watts, known worldwide as Tain, is an American jazz drummer and composer, born in 1960 in Pittsburgh. He studied classical percussion technique at Duquesne University and jazz at the Berklee College of Music, where he met Branford Marsalis. He got the nickname Tain from the pianist Kenny Kirkland, when they drove past a Chieftain petrol station on tour in Florida.

Watts played in Wynton Marsalis's quintet until 1988 and made Grammy-winning albums with it. A year later he joined Branford Marsalis's quartet, with which he again recorded Grammy-winning records. He also played with Michael Brecker, McCoy Tyner, Alice Coltrane, Kenny Garrett, Ravi Coltrane, Betty Carter and many others, and contributed to records by the Mingus Big Band and The Metropolitan Opera. He was also drummer of The Tonight Show for three years and played the jazz musician Rhythm Jones in Spike Lee's Mo' Better Blues.

As a bandleader he writes most of his music himself. His records have appeared since 2007 on his own label Dark Key Music, including Watts, The Impaler and Wattify. In 2017 he received a Guggenheim Fellowship for composition. He is regarded as one of the most influential drummers of the generation after the 1980s.
artiest/jeff-tain-watts.listen: Listen to a recording by the Branford Marsalis Quartet with Watts and notice his drumming: he responds constantly to the soloist and lets the rhythms shift against one another.

artiest/jefferson-airplane.text:
Jefferson Airplane was an American rock band from San Francisco. Singer Marty Balin started the group in 1965 as the house band of his own nightclub The Matrix, a converted pizzeria. He found like-minded musicians in folk singer Paul Kantner, blues guitarist Jorma Kaukonen and later bassist Jack Casady. The name was a joke by Kaukonen, derived from the bluesman Blind Lemon Jefferson. The band began in folk, but soon took inspiration from The Beatles and The Byrds and went electric.

In 1966 the singer Grace Slick joined, from the group The Great Society. She had a powerful, low voice and brought two songs with her: Somebody to Love, written by her brother-in-law, and her own White Rabbit. Both were on Surrealistic Pillow (1967), the album that meant the breakthrough and became one of the most important records of the Summer of Love. White Rabbit uses images from Alice in Wonderland to describe the effects of drugs. The band mixed folk, blues and rock into a psychedelic sound with ripping guitars and multi-part vocals.

Jefferson Airplane was the first band from the San Francisco area to have international success and defined what came to be called the San Francisco Sound. The group played at the great festivals of those years: Monterey Pop in 1967 and Woodstock in 1969. In the early 1970s the band broke up. Kaukonen and Casady carried on as Hot Tuna, Slick and Kantner from 1974 as Jefferson Starship.
artiest/jefferson-airplane.listen: Listen to White Rabbit and follow how the track slowly builds, like a march that grows ever louder and faster. Notice how Grace Slick's voice erupts at the end.

artiest/jelly-roll-morton.text: Ferdinand 'Jelly Roll' Morton was a pianist in the brothels of Storyville in New Orleans and then travelled for years around the United States. He later claimed to have invented jazz; that is not true, but he was the first to take jazz seriously as composition. In 1923, in Richmond, Indiana, he recorded piano solos for Gennett, including King Porter Stomp. In 1926 and 1927 in Chicago, with his Red Hot Peppers, he made records in which solos, breaks and ensemble playing are precisely worked out. In 1938 he spent hours talking and playing about old New Orleans for Alan Lomax of the Library of Congress, also playing rags by Scott Joplin. He died in 1941 in Los Angeles.
artiest/jelly-roll-morton.listen: Notice the breaks: short moments when the band stops and one player carries on alone.

artiest/jelly-roll-morton-s-red-hot-pepp.text:
The Red Hot Peppers were Jelly Roll Morton's recording band, active from 1926 to 1930. Morton formed the group in Chicago as a septet or octet for the label Victor. He brought in the best freelance players of the New Orleans style, including cornettist George Mitchell, trombonist Kid Ory, the clarinettists Omer Simeon and Johnny Dodds and the banjo players Johnny St. Cyr and Bud Scott. In 1928 Morton moved to New York, where he continued recording under the same name, now with musicians from his own band and from other orchestras. In 1930 the name disappeared.

The Chicago recordings of 1926 and 1927 are regarded as the best. Black Bottom Stomp, Smoke-House Blues and Doctor Jazz set a standard for small-group jazz that has still hardly been surpassed. That is due to Morton's work as composer and arranger. The pieces are clearly constructed and yet varied, and they strike a balance between ensemble and solo, with each player given room for a solo of his own.

The records of the Red Hot Peppers also formed an important part of the race records, the record industry for Black audiences in the 1920s and 1930s. They showed how written structure and improvisation can go together, and in doing so gave early jazz an example that later bandleaders followed.
artiest/jelly-roll-morton-s-red-hot-pepp.listen: Listen to Black Bottom Stomp and notice how the band alternates between full ensemble playing and short solos, so that the piece never simply rattles on.

artiest/jemenitisch-joodse-familie-in-je.text:
This is not an artist in the usual sense, but a Yemenite Jewish family in Jerusalem who were recorded in 1955 by Sam Eskin. The names of the singers have not been preserved in the available sources, so the text sticks to what is certain. Eskin was an American folk singer and collector who recorded songs from ordinary people rather than professional musicians.

The recording contains the Hallel, Psalms 113 through 118. This is a series of psalms of praise that in the Jewish tradition are sung or recited on festival days. The Jews of Yemen have for centuries had their own, strictly preserved way of singing. After the founding of Israel, many Yemenite Jews came to the country and brought their liturgical singing tradition with them.

The singing is a communal prayer, not a performance. It is vocal music, often without instruments, with a melody that stays close to the spoken text and repeats in short phrases. Anyone who hears a recording like this hears how a religious text has been passed down orally through the centuries and how the melody carries part of the meaning. For the history of popular music such music matters because it shows that singing and rhythm in many cultures first found their place in community and prayer, long before the first records.
artiest/jemenitisch-joodse-familie-in-je.listen: Listen to the Hallel and notice how the voices often sing in unison and how the melody stays close to the pronunciation of the text. Can you hear how the phrases keep returning?

artiest/jerome-kaltenbach.text:
Jérôme Kaltenbach is a French conductor. From 1979 to 1998 he was music director of the opera company in Nancy, now called the Opéra national de Lorraine. He succeeded Noël Lancien and was himself succeeded by Sebastian Lang-Lessing. In those almost twenty years he headed the orchestra and the opera house on the Place Stanislas.

On record he can be heard in French music of the late nineteenth and the twentieth century. In 1998, for example, he recorded Chausson's Symphony in B-flat, together with the Poème and Viviane, and in 1999 a record of work by Erik Satie, including Parade, Mercure and Relâche and the Trois Gymnopédies. The Satie recordings fit Satie's role in the history of popular music, because his short, bare, repetitive pieces have so often since been heard as a forerunner of minimalist and ambient music.
artiest/jerome-kaltenbach.listen: Listen to Satie's Trois Gymnopédies and notice how little happens: a calm accompaniment and a simple melody that keeps returning.

artiest/jerome-moross.text:
Jerome Moross was an American composer, best known for his film and television music. He was born in 1913 in Brooklyn, to Jewish parents, and became a fine pianist. He formed a lifelong friendship with Bernard Herrmann and in 1931 joined Aaron Copland's Young Composers Group. Herrmann introduced him to the media, beginning with music for radio programmes in 1935. In the 1940s he went to Hollywood, where from 1948 to 1969 he wrote the music for sixteen films.

His best-known film score is the one for The Big Country from 1958, for which he received an Academy Award nomination. According to Moross, he wrote the main title after a memory of a walk across the plain near Albuquerque in 1936. Other films were The Proud Rebel, The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, The Cardinal and The Valley of Gwangi. He also wrote the main theme of the television western Wagon Train. For the theatre he made the musical The Golden Apple (1954), with the song Lazy Afternoon. As an orchestrator he often worked uncredited for others. His symphony was performed in 1943 by Thomas Beecham in Seattle.

His western music has an open, broad sound, with a rhythmic ostinato and syncopation, so that you hear the vast prairie. That sound became a model for the genre and influenced later film composers. Moross died in 1983.
artiest/jerome-moross.listen: Listen to the Main Title of The Big Country and notice the rhythm of the horses and the broad, proud melody in the brass. Can you hear the space of the landscape?

artiest/jerry-dammers.text:
Jerry Dammers is a British keyboard player, songwriter and DJ, born in 1955 in Ootacamund in southern India, the son of a clergyman. When he was two the family moved to England, and via Sheffield he ended up in Coventry at the age of ten. He was successively a mod, a hippie and a skinhead, and drew inspiration from bands such as The Who and The Kinks and from soul. At the art college in Coventry he met the bassist Horace Panter.

In 1977 Dammers started a band that was meant to bring reggae and punk together: first the Coventry Automatics, later The Specials. He deliberately chose a group of Black and white musicians, at a time when that was rare. To release the debut single Gangsters he founded 2 Tone Records, a kind of Motown for ska. The label also launched Madness, The Selecter and The Beat, and had its own visual language of black-and-white checks and the little man in a suit. After the albums The Specials and More Specials, Ghost Town became a number 1 hit in 1981. Three members then left, and Dammers continued as The Special AKA, with the song Free Nelson Mandela.

Dammers was at the cradle of the ska revival: he combined Jamaican rhythms with the energy of punk, political lyrics and the clothing of 1960s mods and rude boys. His music was also a statement against racism. Free Nelson Mandela grew into a song of the anti-apartheid movement, and in 1988 Dammers helped set up the big concert for Mandela's seventieth birthday.
artiest/jerry-dammers.listen: Listen to Ghost Town (1981) by The Specials. Notice the ominous organ sounds and horns and the slow, hollow rhythm, which conjures the image of a town from which life has vanished.

artiest/jerry-goldsmith.text: Jerry Goldsmith was born in 1929 in Los Angeles and was taught by Miklós Rózsa. He began in radio and television at CBS. In the 1960s he brought modernist techniques to Hollywood. For Freud (1962) and Planet of the Apes (1968) he used twelve-tone rows, unusual percussion and playing techniques such as blowing through horns without the mouthpiece. Chinatown (1974) was given a melancholy solo trumpet. For The Omen (1976) he wrote a chorus with a Latin text and won his only Oscar. Alien (1979) and Star Trek: The Motion Picture (1979) followed. Goldsmith wrote in almost every genre and kept searching for new sounds until his death in 2004.
artiest/jerry-goldsmith.listen: Notice the angular rhythms and unusual sounds of the percussion and brass, and compare them with the warm, lonely trumpet of Chinatown.

artiest/jerry-goodman.text:
Jerry Goodman is an American violinist, born in 1949 in Chicago. His parents both played in the strings of the Chicago Symphony Orchestra. He received a conservatoire training and began his career as a roadie for the group The Flock, in which he later played violin. In this way he grew into one of the best-known players of the electric violin in jazz rock.

After his appearance on John McLaughlin's album My Goal's Beyond in 1971 he became a member of the original Mahavishnu Orchestra, until the group broke up in 1973. There he was regarded as a soloist of equal virtuosity to McLaughlin, keyboard player Jan Hammer and drummer Billy Cobham. In 1974 he made the fusion album Like Children with Hammer. From 1985 he recorded three solo records for Private Music, On the Future of Aviation, Ariel and the live album It's Alive, and also toured with Shadowfax and The Dixie Dregs.

In 1993 he joined The Dixie Dregs of guitarist Steve Morse and played on the studio album Full Circle. Later he toured with Gary Husband and played on Dream Theater's Black Clouds and Silver Linings. Goodman showed that the violin can play a role equal to the guitar in loud, electrically amplified music.
artiest/jerry-goodman.listen: Listen to a track by the Mahavishnu Orchestra and notice how the violin and the guitar answer each other almost like two rock guitarists, in fast, sharp lines.

artiest/jerry-leiber.text:
Jerry Leiber was born on 25 April 1933 in Baltimore. In 1950 he met the pianist Mike Stoller in Los Angeles, with whom he would work throughout his career. Leiber wrote the lyrics, Stoller the music. Leiber was then still working in a record shop, and they discovered that they were both mad about blues and rhythm and blues. Still in 1950, Jimmy Witherspoon recorded their first song.

In 1952 they wrote Kansas City and Hound Dog, which they made for the blues singer Big Mama Thornton. Her version became a hit in 1953, and Elvis Presley's rock 'n' roll version from 1956 became far bigger still. For Presley they also wrote Jailhouse Rock (1957), Loving You and King Creole. With their label Spark Records they worked with The Robins, and after the takeover by Atlantic they were also allowed to produce for other labels. In doing so they became more or less the first independent record producers. For The Coasters they wrote Young Blood, Searchin', Yakety Yak and Charlie Brown. Stand By Me, with Ben E. King, and On Broadway were also theirs.

Leiber and Stoller wrote more than seventy hits. Their songs for The Coasters used the funny slang of teenagers and sounded more like little plays than personal love songs. In this way they helped bring rhythm and blues to the large white audience. In 1964 they started the label Red Bird, which focused on girl groups. In 1987 they were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. Leiber died on 22 August 2011.
artiest/jerry-leiber.listen: Listen to Yakety Yak by The Coasters (1958). Notice how the track works like a little play: parents giving their teenager orders, a chorus that talks back and a saxophone that joins in as an extra voice.

artiest/jerry-orbach.text:
Jerry Orbach was an American actor and singer, born in 1935 in the Bronx. His father performed in vaudeville and his mother was a radio singer. He grew up in various cities, took acting lessons at school and in 1955 went to New York to study at the Actors Studio. His career began on the stage, on and off Broadway.

In 1960 he played El Gallo in the first off-Broadway production of The Fantasticks. He was the first to sing the song Try to Remember, which later became a standard in popular music. He made his Broadway debut in Carnival!. He also played Billy Flynn in the first production of Chicago and appeared in 42nd Street. For his role as Chuck Baxter in Promises, Promises he won a Tony Award for best actor in a musical. He was called one of the last true leading men of the Broadway musical.

In the 1980s he worked mainly in film and television, with roles in Prince of the City, Dirty Dancing and Crimes and Misdemeanors. In the Disney film Beauty and the Beast he voiced Lumière. He became known worldwide as Detective Lennie Briscoe in the series Law and Order, which he played from 1992 to 2004. Orbach died at the end of 2004. His place in the history of popular music is that of the musical singer, who with a single production sent a song out into the world.
artiest/jerry-orbach.listen: Listen to Try to Remember from The Fantasticks and notice how it begins as a soft, almost spoken narration with little accompaniment.

artiest/jerry-orbach-en-angela-lansbury.text:
Jerry Orbach and Angela Lansbury were an American and a British actor who both also sang. In the 1991 Disney film Beauty and the Beast they voiced two enchanted household objects: Orbach was the candelabrum Lumière and Lansbury the teapot Mrs. Potts. Together they appear on the soundtrack with the song Be Our Guest, one of the great numbers of the film. The music was by Alan Menken, the lyrics by Howard Ashman.

Orbach was familiar to Broadway audiences, where he played in Chicago among other shows, and later as a detective in the television series Law & Order. Lansbury was a versatile actress with a long career in film, theatre and television. She played the lead in the television series Murder, She Wrote, which ran from 1984 to 1996, lasted twelve seasons and became one of the most successful and longest-running television series ever. She received ten Golden Globe nominations for it, of which she won four. Earlier she appeared in film adaptations of Agatha Christie, including as Miss Marple in The Mirror Crack'd (1980).

For the history of popular music, Be Our Guest matters above all as an example of the new flowering of the Disney musical in the 1990s, in which the songs took on a full role in the story. The song is a showstopper in the style of revue theatre: full of pace, with chorus and large orchestration, and a singer who addresses the audience directly.
artiest/jerry-orbach-en-angela-lansbury.listen: Listen to Be Our Guest and notice the way the singing is written like a stage act: how does the song build from a spoken invitation into a great orchestral feast?

artiest/jerry-wexler.text:
Jerry Wexler was an American music journalist and producer, born in 1917 in the Bronx, New York. He grew up in Washington Heights and as a young man collected 78 rpm records of jazz musicians. After his military service he studied journalism in Kansas. He then worked as an editor at the trade magazine Billboard. There in 1949 he coined the term rhythm and blues, as a replacement for the name race records that the magazine used for the chart of Black music.

In 1953 Wexler became a partner at Atlantic Records, the label of Ahmet Ertegun. Together they made it a major label, with Ray Charles, The Drifters and Ruth Brown. In the 1960s he struck a distribution deal with Stax in Memphis and had artists record in the studios of Muscle Shoals in Alabama, among them Wilson Pickett. In 1967 he brought Aretha Franklin to Atlantic. She had had little success at her previous label, but with Wexler she became the most successful female singer in America within a short time. Later he produced Dusty in Memphis by Dusty Springfield, signed Led Zeppelin and produced Bob Dylan's Slow Train Coming (1979).

Wexler was a producer who put an artist's talent first. He looked for the right musicians and the right studio, and then let the singer have her way. In this way he put Atlantic at the forefront of soul music. Asked what should be on his gravestone, he answered: more bass. He died in 2008.
artiest/jerry-wexler.listen: Listen to I Never Loved a Man (The Way I Love You) (1967) by Aretha Franklin, her first record for Atlantic. Notice how the band plays calmly and sparingly, so that her voice has all the space.

artiest/jess-stacy.text:
Jess Stacy was an American jazz pianist of the swing era. He was born in 1904 in Bird's Point, Missouri. His first piano teacher played piano for silent films. At school he already played in a small jazz group, which in 1921, as Peg Meyer's Melody Kings, toured the Mississippi on riverboats. In the early 1920s he moved to Chicago, where he played with Paul Mares, the leader of the New Orleans Rhythm Kings, in what was later called the Chicago style. His greatest examples were Louis Armstrong and above all the pianist Earl Hines.

In 1935 Benny Goodman asked him to join his band. Stacy stayed until 1939 and was part of the famous Carnegie Hall concert in 1938. During Sing, Sing, Sing (With a Swing), after a duet between Goodman and Gene Krupa, he was unexpectedly given a piano solo. That unplanned, lyrical solo later became famous. He also played with Bix Beiderbecke, Eddie Condon, Bud Freeman, Billie Holiday, Lionel Hampton and Jack Teagarden, and in Bob Crosby's orchestra.

In 1950 he moved to Los Angeles, where his career declined into work in clubs. He stopped performing and worked as, among other things, a salesman and a postman. A brief revival followed in the 1970s. His last performance was broadcast in 1981 on Marian McPartland's Piano Jazz. He died in 1995 and was inducted a year later into the Big Band and Jazz Hall of Fame.
artiest/jess-stacy.listen: Listen to Sing, Sing, Sing (With a Swing) from the 1938 Carnegie Hall concert and notice Stacy's piano solo, which, after Krupa's thundering drums, begins quietly and melodically.

artiest/jesse-saunders.text:
Jesse Saunders is an American house musician, DJ, producer and entrepreneur, born in 1962 and raised on the South Side of Chicago. As a teenager he got to know the city's club scene through Frankie Knuckles. Knuckles played at the Warehouse, where house music originated. In 1982 Saunders opened his own club, the Playground, and added his own material to his disco and R&B sets.

In 1983 he began producing himself. In early 1984, together with Vince Lawrence, he released the single On and On on their own label Jes Say Records. It is regarded as one of the first commercial house singles on vinyl. The track came about as a replacement for a bootleg megamix that had been stolen from his record collection. Saunders and Lawrence used a Roland TR-808 as rhythm machine, a Korg Poly-61 and a Roland TB-303 as bass sound. Funk U Up, the first house track on the Billboard chart, followed, then Real Love, Love Can't Turn Around and Dum Dum. His group Jesse's Gang signed to Geffen and released Center of Attraction, with the club hit I'm Back Again.

Later he concentrated on writing, producing and remixing. He founded the label Broken Records and since 1991 organised the House Music Reunion Picnic. In 2009 the album 25th Anniversary of House Music appeared, followed by a world tour. His importance lies chiefly in the early vinyl: he was one of the first to put house music on record.
artiest/jesse-saunders.listen: Listen to On and On and notice the drum machine and the bass sound: they run on with almost no variation and form the heart of the track.

artiest/jet.text:
Jet is an Australian rock band from Melbourne, formed in 2001 by the brothers Nic and Chris Cester together with the guitarist Cameron Muncey. A year later the bassist Mark Wilson joined. The brothers grew up on their father's records: classic rock from the 1960s and 1970s. Among their influences they count the Beatles, the Rolling Stones, the Faces, AC/DC and T. Rex. Nic sang and played rhythm guitar, Chris drummed.

At the end of 2002 the EP Dirty Sweet appeared on their own label. The first pressing of a thousand copies sold out quickly. A writer for the NME heard in the song Take It or Leave It a mixture of the Rolling Stones and AC/DC. Elektra signed the band. The debut album Get Born was recorded in 2003 in Los Angeles with the producer Dave Sardy, with Billy Preston on keyboards on two tracks. The album reached number one in Australia. The single Are You Gonna Be My Girl became their biggest hit. The Rolling Stones asked Jet to support them on the Australian leg of their tour, and at the 2004 ARIA Music Awards the band won six prizes.

Shine On followed in 2006 and Shaka Rock in 2009, both in the Australian top five. In 2012 the group stopped, but later it came together again. Jet stands for a return to straightforward guitar rock in the early 2000s, with a sound that explicitly referred to the classics of thirty years earlier.
artiest/jet.listen: Listen to Are You Gonna Be My Girl and notice the guitar riff that opens the track and how the drums and the vocals stomp through it, raw and straight.

artiest/jevgeni-mravinski.text:
Jevgeni Mravinski, in English Yevgeny Mravinsky, was a Soviet Russian conductor, pianist and professor at the Leningrad conservatoire. He was born in 1903 in Saint Petersburg. His aunt was the soprano Yevgeniya Mravina. In 1918 he was already working behind the scenes at the Mariinsky Theatre. He first studied biology, but in 1924 went to the conservatoire. His first appearance as a conductor was in 1929.

In 1938 he won the All-Union conducting competition in Moscow and became chief conductor of the Leningrad Philharmonic Orchestra, a post he held until his death in 1988. Under him the orchestra became internationally famous, especially with Russian music. His name is closely linked with Dmitri Shostakovich. He conducted the world premiere of the Fifth Symphony and later also of the Sixth, Eighth, Ninth, Tenth and Twelfth, and of the First Violin Concerto and the First Cello Concerto. He also premiered Prokofiev's Sixth Symphony. For Deutsche Grammophon he recorded Tchaikovsky's symphonies.

On the podium he was austere, with simple, clear gestures, often without a baton. One critic compared his Tchaikovsky to a wild horse that is only just held in check by the will of its master. In a piece Mravinsky sought the atmosphere the composer had intended. Through his premieres he helped determine how Shostakovich was heard in the twentieth century.
artiest/jevgeni-mravinski.listen: Listen to a recording of Shostakovich's Fifth Symphony under Mravinsky and notice the tight, tense sound of the strings and the contrast between quiet and loud passages.

artiest/jim-morrison.text:
Jim Morrison was born on 8 December 1943 in Melbourne, Florida, the son of a naval officer. The family moved often. As a young child he saw, in the New Mexico desert, a road accident with injured Native Americans by the roadside, a memory he later kept bringing back in his songs and poems. His family remembers the incident differently from how he told it.

In 1965 he founded The Doors in Venice, California, with keyboard player Ray Manzarek. Morrison sang and wrote most of the lyrics. After two unremarkable years the band broke through with Light My Fire, from the debut album The Doors (1967), which reached number 1 in America. With Morrison the group made six studio albums, up to and including L.A. Woman. On stage he often recited poems while the band played. His performances were unpredictable and provocative: in 1967 he was arrested on stage in New Haven, and a concert in Miami in 1969 led to court cases.

Morrison combined poetic, dark lyrics with a deep, dark voice. He became a symbol of the counterculture and the generation gap of the 1960s. His drinking sometimes affected his performances. On 3 July 1971 he died unexpectedly in an apartment in Paris, aged 27. Because no autopsy was carried out, the cause of death was never established. In 1993 he was inducted with The Doors into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
artiest/jim-morrison.listen: Listen to Light My Fire (1967). Notice Ray Manzarek's organ intro, the long instrumental middle section with organ and guitar, and Morrison's dark, calm voice around it.

artiest/jim-pepper.text:
Jim Pepper was an American jazz saxophonist, composer and singer with Kaw and Muscogee roots. He was born in 1941 in Salem, Oregon, and grew up in Portland. In 1964 he moved to New York. In the late 1960s he became known as a member of The Free Spirits, an early jazz rock group with Larry Coryell and Bob Moses. That band, active from 1965 to 1968, is regarded as the first to combine jazz and rock. His main instrument was the tenor saxophone; he also played flute, soprano saxophone and percussion, and sometimes sang.

Don Cherry and Ornette Coleman encouraged him to work his heritage into his jazz. The result was a mixture of jazz and Native American music. His best-known piece is Witchi Tai To, based on a peyote song of the Native American Church that he learned from his grandfather. In 1969 he sang it as a member of the group Everything Is Everything. It reached number 69 on the Billboard Hot 100. Later it was covered by many others, including Jan Garbarek and Harpers Bizarre.

Pepper recorded with Don Cherry, Naná Vasconcelos, John Scofield and many others. His CD Comin' and Goin' became the first CD on the new label Rykodisc. In 1998 Gunther Schuller made a version of Witchi Tai To for symphony orchestra and jazz band. Pepper died in 1992. His saxophone and hat are held in the National Museum of the American Indian.
artiest/jim-pepper.listen: Listen to Witchi Tai To and notice how a simple, song-like melody of Native American origin is played and sung within a jazz and rock sound.

artiest/jimi-hendrix.text:
Jimi Hendrix was born on 27 November 1942 in Seattle. After a short spell in the American army he worked for years as an accompanying guitarist, including with The Isley Brothers and in Little Richard's band. In September 1966 Chas Chandler, the former bassist of The Animals, brought him to London. There, with bassist Noel Redding and drummer Mitch Mitchell, he formed The Jimi Hendrix Experience.

The group had immediate success in England with Hey Joe, Purple Haze and The Wind Cries Mary. The debut album Are You Experienced (1967) was kept off the top spot in England only by Sgt. Pepper. Axis: Bold as Love (1967) and the double album Electric Ladyland (1968), his only number 1 in America, followed. At the Monterey Pop Festival in June 1967 he set his guitar on fire at the end of his performance, and at Woodstock in 1969 he played a distorted version of the American national anthem, The Star-Spangled Banner.

Hendrix played left-handed on a flipped right-handed guitar and used volume, feedback and effects pedals as part of the music rather than as an afterthought. He came out of the blues and rhythm and blues, but pulled them towards rock, psychedelia and funk. He died on 18 September 1970 in London, aged 27. His influence extends from hard rock guitarists to jazz musicians such as Miles Davis, who listened to him when he went electric.
artiest/jimi-hendrix.listen: Listen to the beginning of Purple Haze: the two notes grinding against each other form a tritone, an interval long regarded as unsettling. Then notice how the guitar in the solo sounds distorted and almost singing.

artiest/jimmie-nicol.text:
Jimmie Nicol is an English drummer who became known for an exceptionally short job: in June 1964 he replaced Ringo Starr in the Beatles. He was born in 1939 and began his career in 1957, when the impresario Larry Parnes discovered him while he was drumming at the 2i's Coffee Bar in London. He played in various bands and in 1964 founded the Shubdubs, a jazz group in the vein of Georgie Fame and the Blue Flames.

On 3 June 1964, the day before the Beatles were due to begin their tour of Australasia, Starr was admitted to hospital with tonsillitis. Manager Brian Epstein and producer George Martin quickly looked for a replacement. Martin suggested Nicol, whom he had used shortly before at a recording session. George Harrison at first did not want to tour without Starr. Nicol was given a trial session at Abbey Road, a Beatle haircut and an altered suit of Starr's. He gave his first concert less than a day later, in Copenhagen, for 4,500 fans. In all he played eight concerts, until Starr returned on 14 June in Melbourne. He received a cheque for 500 pounds and a gold watch.

After that the attention paid to him quickly faded. In 1965 he went bankrupt. He played with, among others, the Spotnicks and in Mexico and left music in 1975 to become an entrepreneur. His story shows how big Beatlemania was in 1964: the group remained in demand, even with an unknown drummer.
artiest/jimmie-nicol.listen: Listen to a Beatles recording from 1964, such as She Loves You, and notice how the drums carry the tempo: this is the work that Nicol had to take over in a few hours.

artiest/jimmie-rodgers.text:
Jimmie Rodgers was born in 1897 in Meridian, Mississippi, the son of a railway worker. His mother died when he was six, and he grew up with relatives. As a boy he preferred going to vaudeville shows to going to school. At thirteen he won a singing competition and for a time travelled with a touring medicine show. He then worked for years on the railways, first as a water boy for Black work gangs and later as a brakeman. From those workers he learned work songs, blues and banjo playing.

In 1924 he contracted tuberculosis, and in 1927 he left the railway to become a musician. That year he recorded for the producer Ralph Peer of the record label Victor, at the recording sessions in Bristol, Tennessee, where the Carter Family was also discovered. At a second session Blue Yodel No. 1 (T for Texas) came about, a success that made him known all over America. In his short career he recorded more than 120 songs. Rodgers sang blues with a guitar, and let his voice break into a yodel that became his trademark. That is why he was called The Singing Brakeman and America's Blue Yodeler.

Rodgers died in 1933 at the age of 35 of tuberculosis. Even so, he is regarded as the father of country music. He brought together the music of the countryside, the blues of the Black railroad workers and vaudeville, and so became one of the first stars of the genre.
artiest/jimmie-rodgers.listen: Listen to Blue Yodel (T for Texas) and notice the yodel at the end of the verses, where Rodgers lets his voice break. Hear also how the track is built like a blues, with only his guitar as accompaniment.

artiest/jimmy-cliff.text:
Jimmy Cliff was a Jamaican musician in ska, rocksteady, reggae and soul. He was born in 1944 as James Chambers in Saint James and wrote songs as early as primary school. At fourteen he went to Kingston, where he chose his stage name. He persuaded Leslie Kong to start a recording studio with him. In 1964 he represented Jamaica at the World's Fair in New York. He signed to Island Records and moved to the United Kingdom.

His international debut album Hard Road to Travel appeared in 1967. Wonderful World, Beautiful People in 1969 and Vietnam in 1970 followed. In 1969 he wrote Many Rivers to Cross about his struggle with the music industry. With his version of Wild World by Cat Stevens he reached the British top ten. In 1972 he played the lead in The Harder They Come, the first major commercial film from Jamaica. The soundtrack album made reggae known worldwide. Later songs included You Can Get It If You Really Want, Reggae Night from 1983 and a cover of I Can See Clearly Now for the film Cool Runnings.

Cliff deliberately sought a broad audience, including a white one, through record contracts, covers of pop and rock and film music. He became one of the most celebrated musicians of Jamaica and received the Order of Merit, the country's highest honour. He died in 2025. His importance lies in the way he took reggae abroad, first as a singer and then as a film star.
artiest/jimmy-cliff.listen: Listen to The Harder They Come and notice how the story of a young man seeking his chance in Kingston is sung, to a slow reggae rhythm, almost like a narration.

artiest/jimmy-cobb.text:
Jimmy Cobb was an American jazz drummer, born in 1929 in Washington, D.C. As a boy he stayed up at night to hear jazz on the radio from New York, and in the Catholic church he heard church music. In 1950 he began touring with the saxophonist Earl Bostic. He then played with the singer Dinah Washington, the saxophonist Cannonball Adderley and many others, and also with Billie Holiday and Dizzy Gillespie.

In 1958, on Adderley's recommendation, Cobb joined the sextet of the trumpeter Miles Davis. His best-known work is Kind of Blue (1959), on which he formed the rhythm section with bassist Paul Chambers and the pianists Bill Evans and Wynton Kelly. He also plays on Sketches of Spain (1960) and Someday My Prince Will Come (1961). In 1963 he left Davis and formed a trio with Kelly and Chambers, which also worked with the guitarist Wes Montgomery. Later he played in the Great Jazz Trio with Hank Jones and toured with Sarah Vaughan. Only in 1983 did he make his first record as a leader, So Nobody Else Can Hear.

Cobb was a modest drummer who never put himself in the foreground. His playing was subtle: a light, floating rhythm on the cymbals that carries the soloists without disturbing them. As a result he received less attention than other drummers, but musicians such as Davis admired him. After Davis's death he was for a long time the last living musician of Kind of Blue. He died in 2020.
artiest/jimmy-cobb.listen: Listen to So What from Kind of Blue (1959). Notice Cobb's soft, even tap on the cymbals and the single cymbal stroke with which he marks the start of Davis's trumpet solo.

artiest/jimmy-eat-world.text:
Jimmy Eat World is an American rock band from Mesa, Arizona, formed in 1993. Singer and guitarist Jim Adkins and drummer Zach Lind had been friends since kindergarten. Together with guitarist Tom Linton and bassist Mitchel Porter, later replaced by Rick Burch, they began with a punk sound. The name comes from a child's drawing in which Linton's younger brother sees his brother putting the world in his mouth, with the caption Jimmy eat world.

The band released a demo in 1993 and in 1994 the EP One, Two, Three, Four and the debut album Jimmy Eat World. Under the influence of groups such as Sunny Day Real Estate the tempos became slower and the songs more varied. In 1995 the band signed to Capitol Records. Commercial success came with Bleed American (2001), from which four singles reached the top twenty of the Alternative Songs chart, with The Middle at number 1. The 2004 album Futures yielded the number 1 Pain, and Chase This Light (2007) became their highest-charting album. In 2019 the tenth album, Surviving, appeared.

The music combines guitars, melodic choruses and emotional lyrics, in a style later called emo and power pop. Jimmy Eat World is regarded as one of the bands that shaped the guitar sound of the early 2000s. The Middle has an encouraging message about self-confidence that appealed to many young listeners.
artiest/jimmy-eat-world.listen: Listen to The Middle and notice the build-up: how the calm guitar intro grows into a chorus in which all the instruments and the vocals climb together.
